### 1. Lunar Habitat Atmospheric Context
Pressurized rovers and lunar habitats are anticipated to operate under an intermediate atmospheric environment to shorten astronaut pre-breathe protocol times (which otherwise require inhaling 100% $\text{O}_2$ to prevent decompression sickness [F-003]) before extravehicular activities (EVAs) [F-004]. While spacesuits are pressurized with 100% $\text{O}_2$ up to only 4.3 psi [F-001], the expected lunar habitat environment will feature:
* Total pressure: $\le 10.2\text{ psi}$ [F-005]
* Oxygen concentration: $\ge 30\%$ [F-005]

Compared to Earth's sea-level atmosphere, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration, substantially increasing material flammability [F-006].

---

### 2. General Lunar Gravity & Habitat Investigations
* **FM2 Investigation**: Serves as the first-ever combustion experiment on another planetary body, burning four fuel samples at 1/6 lunar gravity inside a sealed chamber under atmospheric conditions planned for future lunar habitats or vehicles [S-025 p.2].
* **SIBAL Fabric / Drop Tower Centrifuge Experiments**: Conducted observations of Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed (SIBAL) fabric (a cotton-fiberglass blend) burning in simulated 1/6 lunar gravity using a drop tower centrifuge [S-025 p.2].

---

### 3. Investigation Relevance Ranking

> **Notice**: The ranking metrics and feature sets listed below originate from an **unverified LLM draft**.

The investigations ranked by relevance to lunar habitat operational conditions are:

1. **FLEX** (Rank 1; Rank Key: 0.591, Score: 0.65)
   * **Matching Features**: Oxygen concentration $\ge 30\%$ (1.0) and total pressure $\le 10.2\text{ psi}$ (1.0) [F-005].
   * **Unknown Features**: Forced flow tested is `unknown`.

2. **ACME-BRE** (Rank 2; Rank Key: 0.5, Score: 0.55) & **ACME-CFI-G** (Rank 3; Rank Key: 0.5, Score: 0.55)
   * **Matching Features**: Oxygen concentration $\ge 30\%$ (1.0) and total pressure $\le 10.2\text{ psi}$ (1.0) [F-005].
   * **Unknown Features**: Forced flow tested is `unknown`.

3. **BASS** (Rank 4; Rank Key: 0.364, Score: 0.364), **BASS-II** (Rank 5; Rank Key: 0.364, Score: 0.364), and **Saffire-I** (Rank 6; Rank Key: 0.364, Score: 0.364)
   * **Matching Features**: Evaluate cabin material fuels (1.0) and forced flow (1.0).
   * **Non-Matching Features**: Do not feature oxygen $\ge 30\%$ (0.0) or total pressure $\le 10.2\text{ psi}$ (0.0).
   * Saffire-I experiment data and diagnostics are documented in PSI records [S-017 p.1], [S-021 p.5].

4. **Saffire-II** (Rank 7; Rank Key: 0.364, Score: 0.667) & **Saffire-III** (Rank 8; Rank Key: 0.364, Score: 0.667)
   * **Matching Features**: Evaluate cabin material fuels (1.0) and forced flow (1.0). Saffire-III diagnostics and data are detailed in repository records [S-017 p.1], [S-021 p.5].
   * **Unknown Features**: `same_test_lunar_atmosphere` and `pressure_at_or_below_10.2psi` are `unknown`.

5. **SAME-R** (Rank 9; Rank Key: 0.273, Score: 0.75) & **DAFT** (Rank 10; Rank Key: 0.182, Score: 0.667)
   * **Matching Features**: Cabin material fuel (1.0).
   * **Unknown Features**: Parameters such as `same_test_lunar_atmosphere`, `o2_at_or_above_30pct`, `pressure_at_or_below_10.2psi`, and `forced_flow_tested` (for DAFT) are `unknown`.

facts.claim: Spacesuits are pressurized with 100% oxygen up to only 4.3 psi.
To prevent decompression sickness ('the bends'), astronauts perform a pre-breathe protocol by inhaling 100% oxygen to purge dissolved nitrogen from body tissues.

To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.

[Saffire-I | S-017: Saffire-I and Saffire-III Description of Data (DoD) & Operations | Data Description & Operations]
There are various documents and associated information located on the different tabs within the SAFFIRE Investigations records in PSI. A very useful document to review first is the “SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf” document located on the “Overview” tab in the Summary Document section. The experiment records are found on the “Data” tab in the SAFFIRE-II Investigations record. Table 1 contains list of experiment records in PSI and a short description of what each record contains. Table 1. Saffire-I/III Experiment Data in PSI Each Experiment Data record contains raw data and multiple image sets. Associated raw data documents and individual image sets are located on the “Scientific Data and Information” tab within the Experiment Data record. The raw data is captured from each experimental sensor and presented in excel files. The suite of experimental sensors used is summarized in Table 2. Table 2. Saffire, I, II and III Diagnostics Table 3 contains a description of the different SAFFIRE image sets loaded in PSI. Table 3. SAFFIRE Image Sets in PSI Some image sets are very large. They may contain over 10,000 images which makes it impractical to display as thumbnails in the Image Gallery which appears on the “Image Data and Information” tab of the Videos & Images record of the image set. In the case of very large image sets, all the images are provided in zip files labeled “Original Image Files” on the “Image Data and Information” tab. These files can be downloaded and viewed on the local machine.

[General | S-025: NASA Microgravity Combustion Program Overview | Background]
Background
FM2 is the first-ever combustion experiment to be performed on another planetary body. Building on the
success of the decades-long combustion science ground (1g) program and International Space Station
(ISS) microgravity (~0g) combustion experiment campaigns, FM2 investigates burning materials on the
Moon at its 1/6 reduced gravity level. Previous computational modeling, bolstered by experiments aboard
parabolicflight aircraft and the ISS, suggest that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in
lunar gravity compared to Earth. This means that some things that are not flammable on Earth, may be
flammable in potential habitats on the Moon and other places with reduced gravity. Since fire can be a
catastrophic hazard for spaceflight and extreme human exploration, FM2 is a critical step in determining
material flammability and safety for future missions.

[General | S-025: NASA Microgravity Combustion Program Overview | Approach and Hardware]
Approach and Hardware
External view of FM2 engineering hardware. External view of FM2 engineering hardware. The experiment burns four fuel samples individually in atmospheric conditions planned for future lunar
habitats or vehicles. The experiment is housed inside a sealed chamber and operates autonomously
through software. Cameras record flame characteristics including size, intensity, color, and spread rate. Onboard sensors measure flame and fuel temperatures, oxygen concentration, and carbon-dioxide
concentrations. Images of FM2 engineering hardware that is 28.5 by 28.5 by 38.5 cm tall. Weight is 25 kg. Internal view of
FM2 engineering hardware. Internal view of FM2 engineering hardware.

[Saffire-I | S-021: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status | 2.2 Diagnostics]
Because of the
importance of addressing these remaining needs to crew
safety in exploration missions, AES management
authorized the SFS Demo project to plan for three more
Saffire experiments, Saffire-IV, V, and VI, that will
address objectives not achieved in Saffire-I-III. Of
particular note is that many of these objectives require
supporting ground-based experimentation to perform
the parametric investigations that are required to fully
understand the phenomena in question. The objective of
the flight experiment is to anchor the ground-based
experiments with flight data. While the planning for the follow-on experiments is
underway, the development process is intended to
mirror the processes executed with Saffire-I-III. The
Mission Concept Review/System Requirements Review is planned for June 2016 with a design review planned
for December 2016.

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
